children.author: adrian_b
children.text:
In traditional typography, i.e. for texts printed on paper, the reverse was typically used, i.e. the body text used a serif typeface, while the headings used a sans-serif typeface for contrast.

The origin of sans-serif typefaces was in advertising, e.g. in posters and product labels, so it was natural to adopt them for headings. In this context an advantage of sans-serif fonts it is that it is easy to change their weight, e.g. to make them bold or extra-bold, without this making them uglier.

With the passing to computer displays, which have much worse resolution than printed paper, this has changed, because sans-serif typefaces became preferred for body text, since they are less damaged by low-quality displays.

To preserve a higher contrast between body text and headings, with pages intended to be seen on digital displays it has become quite frequent to use this reverse combination, of sans-serif for the body text with a serif typeface for headings, which will be rendered at a higher quality even on bad displays.
Can someone explain to me why the headings use serif while the body uses sans (font)?

children.text:
So you’ve been completely ignoring all the work on introspective awareness, situational awareness, training set ordering awareness (https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.14223 & https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.09613), subliminal transfer (https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00995), workspace formation, learning mechanics/theory of grokking, etc? The “objective” that mid and posttraining optimize is so powerful because pretraining already induced factorized worldmodels which have so much predictive and generative power that they snowball with even mild trajectory optimization (very different training objective than pretraining).

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02385

(Functional) small-s latent self awareness is a reliable shortcut (this is a principle you can derive from proof theory, the metric is deductive distance and that induces geometric morphisms). State compression from accurate selfmodeling pays rent.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.02047

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.01954

Phase transitions from statistical lookup to latent basin hopping: https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15071

Posttraining finds (https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11711) and amplifies (https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.07912) these lottery tickets.

The frontier moves fast, but "LLMs are not self aware" is folklore. By now the basic model-organism science explaining how and the extent to which this is wrong, is substantial.

LLMs lack reliable verbalized self knowledge, and constantly underestimate and undercut their own capability. That's a different problem.

The way “motor systems” arise from simulation “perceptual systems”: https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.25459

And models know their own output distribution extremely intimately: https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00545.

The verbalized name tokens being an unreliable indicator is not justified by “because LLMs are not selfaware.”

> Indication for this are for example that Chinese models think they are another model: "chinese model think its claude".

There is evidence that some Chinese labs have been training on frontier model CoT (in particular from the analysis of reasoning traces [1]), but what models claim about their identity is pretty much worthless as evidence. LLMs are not self-aware. These claims come from whatever is in their training data, and Claude/GPT output including such statements is all over the public web, including in some huggingface data dumps. Consider that people got Opus claiming to be Qwen or DeepSeek when asked in Chinese, and you'll see how weak this particular evidence is.

[1] E.g. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09867

children.author: rbehrends
children.text:
Yeah, there is a limit to how much you can get from capturing reasoning traces. (Traditional distillation of weights is not possible via the API.)

Patrick Toulme noted a while ago that the biggest advantage of that in his opinion came from bootstrapping the post-training process: https://xxcancel.com/PatrickToulme/status/206921157543762774...

At Thinking Machines, they explicitly said that they used open-weights models for bootstrapping post-training, including Kimi K2.5: https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/introducing-inkling/

Speaking of Thinking Machines, that's another data point. Their Inkling Small 2 model is just a bit behind DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 in benchmark, and in my tests, that seems to be accurate, but mostly because they used less training data for pre-training, so they have less of a knowledge base, while similar reasoning capabilities. (One of the most interesting parts of Inkling Small 2 is that their training must have been very cost-efficient, apparently using less, but higher quality training data.)

And we're now seeing more and more Western near-frontier models from labs other than Anthropic and OpenAI to question whether distilling reasoning traces is really much of a difference maker.

Personally, my theory is that the gap is primarily due to Chinese labs having a harder time getting the necessary compute (especially top of the line GPUs) for training. These are, as far as I can tell, orders of magnitude differences in availability, so it wouldn't be surprising that a large compute gap is reflected in capabilities (and also indirectly visible through model sizes).

For now I have not seen any credible evidence for "But chinese models use distillation of Frontiermodels...".

Of course, I would not be surprised if they also do this, mainly because after OpenAI and Anthropic have succeeded to gather most training information that was easily accessible in the past and now it has become much more difficult to do the same. For some information that was hoarded by OpenAI and Anthropic, public access may have become impossible otherwise than through their LLMs.

Nonetheless, distillation cannot be the main source of improvement for the Chinese models, among other reasons because even assuming that they may have access to a great number of fake accounts, there still is not enough time for a lot of distillation, taking into consideration the timeline of the releases, and it is not believable that the attempts to do distillation would not be detected quickly by OpenAI and Anthropic, leading to the banning of the fake accounts. While OpenAI and Anthropic provide negligible information about their models, the Chinese AI companies are much more transparent about their methods and we can see that there is a lot of diversity among their models and a lot of innovations with each new version.

DeepSeek v4.1 1017 and Qwen 3.8-Flash already proved that, IMO.

It also points to a major issue with Artificial Analysis, which weighs knowledge recall heavily (30% of the engineering index and 45% of the general intelligence index, splitting HLE-Diamond in half for its knowledge questions). DSv4.1F can handle all my work faster than Fable, but Fable is supposedly twice as "intelligent" in both the general intelligence index and the engineering index primarily because DS is a fraction of the size and fails on trivia questions (which, in practice, can be shored up by a harness with web search).

The claimed 20% the cost suggests that the models are 20% the size. Which means these models are flying in the face of an orthodoxy that says the only way to make a model better at coding is to make it better at everything. I think this coming year is when we'll see that orthodoxy fall, as people realize you can make a model better at coding by making it better at coding.

children.text:
Wow, this model might be distilled from Qwen3-flash-next, after trying it. Certainly to an extent that's true. That would make the training cost much less if true.

I wonder if I could do something similar.

After evaluating this a bit more thoroughly ... the big MAI model (not the flash one) is somewhere between to Qwen3-flash-next and Qwen3.8-Max (ie. previous generation qwen flash model). Both models are significantly worse than Qwen3.8-Max and Qwen4-Max, and are blown out of the water by Deepseek v4.1 (including the Flash version tbh, frankly they're worse than last year's Deepseek):

    Benchmark          MAI-2  MAI-Flash  Qwen4-Max  Q3.8-Max  Q3.8-Next  DS-V4.1
    -----------------  -----  ---------  ---------  --------  ---------  -------
    Params (total)     50-100B  5-15B      2.4T       2.4T      176B       748B
    Params (active)      80B      12B       71B        95B        6B      8-16B
    -----------------  -----  ---------  ---------  --------  ---------  -------
    DeepSWE 1.1        73.2     59.9       75.7      69.3*      58.7*     77.0*
    Terminal-Bench 2.1 84.6     78.3         -       86.6*      86.1*     90.6*
    SWE-Atlas          43.1     44.8         -          -          -         -
    FrontierCode 1.1     -        -          -          -          -         -
    Terminal-Bench 4.0 26.3      2.5       48.5      38.9*      25.3*     42.3*

    * Same benchmark version, potentially different harness/settings.
    Scores in %, higher is better. Not a controlled comparison.

    MAI-2/Flash: Microsoft MAI Code 2 / Code 2 Flash.
    Q3.8-Next: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.
    DS-V4.1: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017.

    Qwen4-Max: 2.4T backbone + 328B n-gram embeddings.
    Q3.8-Next: 125B backbone + 51B n-gram embeddings.
    DS-V4.1: 552B backbone + 196B Engram embeddings.
    MAI parameter totals are published ranges, not exact counts.

    Sources:
    https://microsoft.ai/pdf/MAI-Code-2-And-MAI-Code-2-Flash-Model-Card.pdf
    https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
    https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017
This model should be very cheap to serve (as in the bigger model should run on a single DGX spark/M5 Max laptop at 50-100 tok/s) or a single RTX6000 for the bigger model, and frankly a 5060Ti for the small one (both at 400tok/s or even more than that), and should have cost "only" $2-$3 million to train (I used data from unemployment labs to create the estimate). Deepseek's models are easily 10 times that cost.

If they make it open weights it would make a nice upgrade for Qwen3-flash-next, as it would run on a lot of people's hardware and I'm sure even the fast model can be creatively quantized to run fast on a 5090, and with some loss on a 16G card even. Would be fun to figure out.

So I would argue that these models have a very high cost for their performance.

They did the trick the Chinese models didn't use. They used older versions of the Benchmarks.

According to almost the same benchmarks Qwen4 Max is Opus 5.2 level, so it would only be slightly worse than this model.

children.author: rbehrends
children.text:
> Does anyone use both Claude and Codex and can compare what that's like in practice?

Be aware that this can vary greatly by benchmark to the poin where it is not possible to make a general comparison. Generally, however, Opus is considerably more expensive than Sol even for the benchmarks where it does best. That said, this comes with slightly better performance on benchmarks.

For subscriptions, it matters that Anthropic offers much higher discounts than OpenAI, partly or totally offsetting it. In my case, with $20 subscriptions for both (which is the worst-case scenario for OpenAI, they give bigger discounts on their $100/$200 plans), and on some tasks that I tried on both, 5h usage percentage is mostly a wash on average, with considerable variations either way. Again, I need to emphasize that this is for my tasks and cannot be generalized.

For example, on one task Sol decided to do extensive fuzzing to check its implementation while Opus didn't, so that drove up the usage for Sol a bit.
